questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Charles University has a large selection of courses, for which diversity was the key for me. The courses average 5 ECTS, making it possible for me to choose 6 different courses, in constrast to courses at the Humanities at University of Copenhagen, where all courses are 15 ECTS. My philosophy degree has thus far been saturated with the analytical anglo-saxon school, fundamentally uninterested in art, history, literature, cinema, and culture and society in a broader more nuanced sense, so finally being able to explore these other fields in connection with philosophy was of crucial importance for me. Charles University is also a part of the 4+EU program, which made me think my enrollment would be smooth, avoiding any bureaucratic stop-blocks.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Yes - any trouble I had was largely my own fault for not reading through all the information given or seeking help in time.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I do not quite remember, but there were several emails with information sent to me, such as a comprehensive newsletter involving sight-seeing, information about the university facilities and student organizations and activities.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I am not sure, whether the dorm I was ascribed to is to be considered "on" or "off" campus, but I could not choose which dorm I would like, and only a double shared room was offered to me. It seems one should have made a request in advance, but no information was directly given to me in relation to this. I should have done some research prior to my exchange.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Sadly, there was only one kitchen with a single stove (which tended not to work properly in some periods) and a single sink for a total of 40 people, which is clearly not ideal, but the rent was so low, that I guess I could not expect anything better.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: That they should research the types of dorms they can be ascribed to, and whether it is best for them to seek out housing on their own. I myself considered moving out of the dorm immediately after arriving, but eventually got used to it, largely due to the generosity and friendliness of the folks I was living with. Finding housing on your own gets expensive if one does not search for it at least half a year in advance, if not a whole year, and no information is given on this crucial part of the exchange.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I do not remember in detail. It started off with an application prioritizing the possible institutions and filling it in with courses (which probably would not be availible during the semester abroad). After the acceptance, a learning agreement had to be filled in, as well as a pre-approval of courses, both of which I had to revise and send in again, when I finally knew exactly which courses I was taking.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I do not remember, but with the existence of the internet, help can always be found, albeit not always in the most convenient places.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: The registration process at Charles is quite atrocious with course registration opening at an exact hour at which all students register at the same time, making the site crash continously, having to refresh over and over again, until the site was availible. Luckily I was ready then, but it took me over an hour to enroll in all my courses. With regard to my host institution, University of Copenhagen, the registration simply consisted of a pre-approval of courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: No concrete advice at all.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The bachelor degree in philosophy is really a degree in the analytical anglo-saxon school of philosophy, which excludes the many other schools of thought to the point of not allowing a free discussion, since the discourse of analytical philosophy is centred around a certain way of forming arguments and using concepts. The history of philosophy courses were extremely unambitious and basic to the point of making the lectures superfluous if one had already read and thought through the texts themselves. In addition, there was no oppertunity to read an entire work, everything being presented in excerpts. Because of the strict academic writing style of the analytical school of thought, not a single student is taught how to write in a general manner, where one can find their own style of writing and style of thought. The students enrolled end up being carbon-copies of each other in terms of intellectual output and expression, all being able to write an academic article, but no one being able to write anything compellingly original and thought-provoking, with the ability to reach out to a broader audience. At some points, I wondered whether the university takes its students for a bunch of idiots, who learn so slowly and lack the ability for any kind of creativity, so that the courses are necessarily unambitious and the exams focused on remembering things, proving ones ability to think a thought that has already been thought, instead of doing that and further thinking it through, adding to it, reflecting on it and doing philosophy themselves. Dreaming, wondering, being puzzled and speculating are all discouraged. I am happy to have made friends with my fellow students, with which I have been able to spend valuable and fruitful time doing just that, and in collaboration and on my own developing my own thought, and seeing the philosophers and texts come to full fruition through endless free dialogue and a polyphony of voices entertwining.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of courses suited me well, although the two philosophy courses I took could not balance the level of complexity in the seminars, since a lot of non-philosophy students participated as well. One of the courses was even at an MA-level, from which I expected a lot more intense engagement.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There was much more focus on discussion, and discussion which tolerated many viewpoints and a plurality of ways of expressing oneself. Philosophy at the University of Copenhagen lacks such an open and free space of vigor and critical engagement not governed by an exclusionary principle of "rationality" or a formal "reasonable" way of expression - both concepts here being very spurious and tending to counteract exactly what they try to foster; an open productively engaging discussion.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
1. Literature: on U.S. fin de siécle (turn of the 19th to 20th century) fiction, centring around a kind of decadence of bourgeoise life, where traces of the capitalism life-world and critiques of capitalism in the terms of Debord's idea of "Society of the Spectacle" and Baudrillard's notion of "Consumer Society" can be found.
2. Film: Theoretical study of post-war cinema in relation to postmodernism and countless other analyses and critiques of society and the world of the late 20th century (to today) at large, including many philosophical theoretical texts and the live-viewing of films at the Film Academy, where the discussion were immensily fruitful.
3. History: On the relationship between literature and history, dealing with a plurality of theoretical texts trying to understand the fact that history is something written, how it strives towards a "neutrality", what this neutrality is, what "narrative" is, and how the structure of narrative (most exemplary in myths) invades the writing of history, and in addition what we mean by "history" at all, and what the purpose of history even is.
4. Latin: Reading of latin texts from the golden and silver age of roman literature, focused on improving grammar skills and the ability to interpret inside a historical context. Great practice in terms of the language and beneficial for the enlargement of historical knowledge of the period itself.
5. Philosophy of Image: On what an "image" is, through the phenomenological tradition; Husserl, Heidegger, Derrida, Merleau-Ponty, Henry, Deleuze, as well as a study of the paintings of Van Gogh, Cezanne and Bacon. A critical engagement with the school of phenomenology, historically and theoretically, and fruitful free-form discussions of the approaches of the different thinkers and the role of phenomenology and philosophy as a whole.
6. Philosophy of Personhood: What is a "person", a critical engagement with the historical roots of the concept itself, from Christianity and Trinitarian theology by way of Boethius, focusing on medieaval philosophy, namely Thomas Aquinas and John Duns Scotus, comparing them to a modern thinker, Edith Stein, and her balancing of the phenomenological approach to the concept, bordering on theological and speculative thinking.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: All the courses I took, but especially courses offered at the Department of Anglophone Studies, where all the courses are in English. In the case of someone knowing Czech, I would recommend the many exciting philosophy courses, which I lacked the knowledge of Czech to participate in, sadly.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The kitchen at the dorms were frequently occupied and the dorms were in general not comfortable to spend time at, so I often ate out, which cost more, but I had the money for it, luckily, since the rent was so low. A lot of money was spent on beer and coffee though.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Especially the transport was cheap, as well as taking the train to different parts of the Czech Republic as well as nearby countries. Almost everything was cheaper than in Copenhagen, but I ended spending a lot more money than originally planned, since I came into the habit of spending time at cafes, bars and restaurants, and even though it was cheap I frequented a bit too often, and it became costly. But it was very enjoyable living such a life, and I had the money to do it. With hindsight, I still would have controlled myself a bit more...

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not participate in a lot student-activities, but Prague is a great city and I found a lot of great places to spend time at.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I do not know, I did not look for anything of the sort.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Again, I do not know any specific student activities, but since the university facilities are in the Old Town, you meet a lot of your fellow student and friends from the dorm very often, which was great! Hanging around the centre of the city on various cafes was a great pleasure. In Copenhagen, the University is a bit off to the south of the centre and feels very empty culturally and historically.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Just walk around, the city is very "touristy", so exploring (or simply just revisiting the same places over and over) different parts of the city outside tourist season is very fulfilling. Use the train often to visit other parts of the Czech Republic!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Fairly easy. I wish I had spent more time on learning Czech though. I could have reached a level, where I could steadily practice it day by day, reaching a good knowledge and practice of it by the end of the semester, but I started engaging with the language quite late into the semester (mainly because the language courses were places in the same time-slots as my other courses).

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Going aborad is a great practice in socializing, and at the end I feel more courageous engaging with all sorts of people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not anything in particular. The culture is very European, and because of my slavic background, the non-European culture mainly being slavic, I was pleasantly surprised by recognizing a lot of things.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Going to cafes and bars regularly, as well as independant music-venues.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Do research on the housing availible and consider finding housing on your own, knowing that the housing at the dorms is very bad.
2. Take a plurality of courses in different fields if possible, and watch out for which language is course is taught in. Know that one can enroll in many courses and then un-enroll during the first couple of weeks; see what suits you best.
3. Participate in some extra courses without searching for pre-approval (knowing that you will not get points) just purely for interest - watch out though, because the intensity of the courses vary a lot!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The three mentioned above are the most crucial. Also, Prague might be the best European city to study abroad in. I would only recommend something in France, Italy, Germany, Spain and Portugal, if part of your plan is to learn the language as well, but without a plan to achieve a certain degree of fluency, taking courses in the native language as well, Prague is simply the best place.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Learning to socialize more and realizing how much more crucial non-academic discussions are to developing one's own way of thinking, and listening to so many points of view, which are not to be found inside academia.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The dorms were hard to get used to.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
